observations.text: "Give me life" is the most frequent prayer in this unit
observations.meaning: "Give me life" is the most frequent prayer in this unit (15 of the 22 face-N hits are Psalm 119). Each asks for life on a named ground: "according to your word", "in your ways", "in your righteousness", "in your steadfast love", "according to your justice", "according to your promise", "according to your rules". The asking comes out of a condition: "My soul clings to the dust; give me life according to your word!"; "I am severely afflicted; give me life, O Lord, according to your word!"

observations.text: Death as a sleep not roused.
observations.meaning: Setting: Job sets a man against a tree. The tree has hope from its own root; the man has none from himself. Meaning: death is named as sleep, and the sleep has no waking "till the heavens are no more". Implies (R): I read the limit, "till the heavens are no more", as a boundary set on the not-waking rather than an open "never". Job does not draw it out. What he does is turn at once from the fact to God: hide me, appoint a time, remember me, call, and I will answer. The hope he cannot find in nature, he asks of God. The verses state both the despair (14:12) and the asking (14:13–15), side by side.
observations.note: October disposition: W / NS (§F, decision 1) (_analytics/Clusters/M25 - life-death/life-death-observation-ledger-unit4-v1-20261004.md)

observations.text: Sheol roused to greet the dead king.
observations.meaning: Setting: a taunt (14:4), a song mocking a fallen tyrant. Meaning: the point is his fall. The great of the earth meet him only to say he is now as weak as they are, and his body lies among maggots. Implies: it speaks of pride brought down by death ("Your pomp is brought down to Sheol"). Because it is a taunt, I do not read it as a teaching on the state of the dead. It is the third kind of verse about the dead, beside "the dead know nothing" (Ecc 9:5) and the dead with God (Luk 16:22).

Against it stands the Lord, who is present ("in his holy temple"), and the right answer to him is silence, not a call to wake.

observations.text: God called to awake when life is sought.
observations.meaning: Counted: of the five psalms in which a person calls God to "awake" with this word (Psa 7; 35; 44; 59; 80), all five carry life, by context: four have the speaker's life sought or taken, and Psa 80 ends "give us life". Meaning: the call to God to wake rises where life is under threat. Implies (R): I read the cry as speaking from how it feels when God does not act: "Why are you sleeping, O Lord?" Scripture states elsewhere that "he who keeps Israel will neither slumber nor sleep" (Psa 121:4, another word). The two stand side by side, unreconciled. Paul quotes Psa 44:22 and answers it: "No, in all these things we are more than conquerors through him who loved us" (Rom 8:36–37).

observations.text: The dead waking.

observations.text: Psalm 49: two ends for the soul.
observations.meaning: Setting: the psalm is about death that comes to everyone, the wise and the fool alike (49:10). It is not about escaping a danger in life. Meaning: set against that death, the psalmist says God will ransom his soul from Sheol's power, "for he will receive me". Of the rich man who trusts in his wealth, "his soul will go to the generation of his fathers, who will never again see light." Implies: here the soul has an end beyond death, and there are two ends: received by God, or gone to the fathers in the dark. What the psalm sets against each other is two souls, not soul and spirit. It does not say what "receive" involves. (The same verb is used of Enoch: "God took him", Gen 5:24. I note this; I do not draw it in.)
